item.title: The eMudhra issue was so bad, it delayed Fedora 45 until November at the earliest
item.itunes:title: The eMudhra issue was so bad, it delayed Fedora 45 until November at the earliest
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Fedora 45 delayed to Nov 3 due to four blockers, including compromised eMudhra certs.
  • eMudhra issued trivially factorable private keys; Fedora must update intermediates before release.
  • Other blockers: LVM autoactivation, Plasma Discover serving outdated RPMs, Stratis encrypted pool boot failure.

If you haven't heard the news already, there was a major security concern with website certificates. The issuer, eMudhra, had distributed very easy-to-crack private keys, with the worst offender simply being the number "4." Well, it seems this issue has convinced the Fedora community to hold off on the release of version 45, as it was one of four reasons why the release is now a No-Go until November.

Fedora 45's release is delayed until November, partially due to the eMudhra issue

Three other problems were standing in its way

As spotted by Phoronix, the Fedora community has opted to delay the release of Fedora 45 until November. Whenever a new major version of Fedora is on the horizon, the community can vote to put up what it calls "blockers." These are concerns or issues the people have with releasing the new version of Fedora. If there are enough blockers deemed worthy of concern, the release is delayed until the blockers are cleared.

At the time of writing, there are four blockers in place, and one of them directly mentions the recent eMudhra problem:

"You probably heard of the compromised eMudhra certificates which had very easy to factor private keys.

I think this can be serious for some users, a quick update would be beneficial for all the users of Fedora. I did not see any updates in Bodhi yet."

The blocker documentation points to the website eMudhra We Have A Problem, which tells you if your computer accepts the compromised intermediates. The documentation claims that Fedora currently accepts them, and that has to be fixed before 45 can be rolled out.

Of course, that's just one of four active blockers. The other three include LVM autoactivation failing after the Fedora 45 upgrade, Plasma Discover grabbing outdated RPMs for Fedora 44, and the Stratis encrypted pool failing to boot. The release has been pushed to November 3rd to give the community time to fix all the problems.

item.title: I let a local LLM control my Home Assistant automations, and it took a wrong turn before I added guardrails
item.itunes:title: I let a local LLM control my Home Assistant automations, and it took a wrong turn before I added guardrails
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I already use a local LLM with Home Assistant to handle requests that its built-in voice commands don’t understand. Most of what I say still goes through regular intent matching, but having a model interpret more complex requests makes the setup much more convenient. I can phrase things naturally and have it select an existing routine without remembering the exact command. Once that works, giving a local model more control over your automations is a tempting next step.

The trouble is that a model’s interpretation determines what happens in your house, and the local model isn't always as accurate as you'd expect it to be. It's also not the smartest. It has messed up plenty of times for me. Sometimes, it's small things like switching off the lights when I ask for the lamps to be switched off, even though I'm using the correct words that I've assigned. There have been plenty of such cases, and they've now forced me to add guardrails.

Connecting the model is fairly straightforward

I’m using Qwen3 1.7B on my Mac

I’m using Qwen3 1.7B on my Mac, with Home Assistant running on a separate machine. The model doesn’t need to run on the same hardware as Home Assistant. You can serve it over your local network and configure a conversation integration to send requests to it.

Ollama is one way to do this. You run the model on your Mac, make the server accessible over your local network, and add the Ollama integration in Home Assistant under Settings > Devices & services. Since the two are running on separate machines, the server address needs to point to your Mac’s local IP address. You then select the model and use the conversation agent in your voice assistant configuration.

The integration’s “Control Home Assistant” option lets the model use Home Assistant’s tools to interact with the entities you expose to Assist. These can include bedroom lights, individual lamps, fans, and thermostats. The model interprets your request, chooses a tool and its parameters, and Home Assistant executes it.

Existing routines can also be made available through scripts. For example, a bedtime script could switch off the TV and living-room lights, then leave a bathroom light on briefly. Exposing that script gives the model a way to start the sequence when you ask it to get the house ready for bed. The script’s description tells it what the routine does and when to use it.

I’ve given my model access to quite a few things. That expands the requests it can handle, but it also gives a 1.7-billion-parameter model more devices and actions to choose between whenever I ask it to do something.

Local LLMs changed how I use Home Assistant, and now my smart devices actually listen

Local LLMs made my Home Assistant setup far more responsive than any app or integration

3
By  Ayush Pande

The model sometimes gets basic requests wrong

The most annoying mistakes are the ones that are most basic

The most annoying mistakes involve commands that should be straightforward. I ask it to switch off the lamps, and the model switches off the lights instead. I’m already using the names I’ve assigned, so there isn’t much more I can do to make that particular request clearer. Yet it happens often enough that I have to pay attention to what the assistant actually does.

I’ve also had questions turn into actions. Asking whether a light is on should get me an answer about its current state, but the model has triggered my “Good night” helper instead. Command scope is another recurring problem. There are times when a request meant for the lights in one room ends up affecting lights across the house. Switching them all back on doesn’t undo the mistake properly either, because some were already off.

Then there are requests where the assistant doesn’t execute anything. I’ve had it read the function-call syntax aloud instead of performing the action. Now, most of these mistakes aren't deal breakers, and they don't happen all the time. But when they do, they set you back and force you to fix whatever the command broke. And if it's an elaborate automation, like a nighttime routine, you've just got yourself a whole chore to deal with before bed, which has happened to me quite a bit.

You need to limit what the model can do

I am now very careful with what it can access

After dealing with these mistakes enough times, I eventually started adding guardrails to my setup. One thing I've learned is that simply telling the model not to do something isn't enough. For example, you can add a line to your system prompt telling it never to switch off every light in the house unless explicitly asked, but you're still relying on the same model to interpret that instruction correctly. If you want to prevent something from happening, put those restrictions in the tools and automations that actually execute the commands.

First, I limited what the model could access in Home Assistant. Home Assistant itself recommends exposing fewer than 25 entities when experimenting with local models, and that's a good starting point. I've kept the lights, devices, and routines I use regularly available to the model, but there's no reason to give it access to everything in my house. You also need to be careful about which scripts and helpers you expose. A seemingly harmless script could trigger several other automations, so you're effectively giving the model control over more devices than you intended.

Another thing that has helped is using predefined scripts for anything involving multiple devices. Take my bedtime routine, for example. Instead of letting the model decide which lights to switch off, what temperature to set, and how long the bathroom light should stay on, I use a script that handles it all. The model only needs to recognize my request and trigger that script. Everything else happens in a sequence I've already defined and tested.

Of course, that doesn't mean you should blindly trust every command the model sends to a script. I've also found it important to restrict what these tools can actually do. For example, you can configure a thermostat tool to reject temperatures outside a certain range or make a lighting tool accept commands for only a particular room. The key is that the script or tool itself must enforce these checks. For more sensitive actions, I'd rather require confirmation through a trusted interface or simply keep those controls out of the model's reach.

I’m keeping the model on a leash

I still want the convenience of speaking naturally to my home, but I don’t trust this model with unrestricted control. The mistakes are too frequent for that. If you’re trying something similar, decide exactly what it can operate before expanding access.

I made my smart home even smarter with a couple of Home Assistant add-ons

I now have a local AI chatbot that I can speak to.

item.title: I replaced Notion, Obsidian Bases, and Trello with one powerful Docker container
item.itunes:title: I replaced Notion, Obsidian Bases, and Trello with one powerful Docker container
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have lost count of how many productivity tools I have experimented with over the years. Notion was my go-to for organizing information. Obsidian Bases also looked promising, and Trello kept my projects moving with its intuitive Kanban boards and automations.

Each tool had its strengths, but I wanted something that brought the best of all three under one roof, without another subscription or compromising control over my data. That’s when I came across a powerful open-source Docker container that changed my approach: Baserow.

7 best Docker containers for productivity

Best containers to get things done

4
By  Parth Shah

Getting started with Baserow is straightforward

Took me just 10 minutes

One of the reasons I love Docker is how easy it makes deploying powerful self-hosted applications, and Baserow is no exception. I headed to Baserow’s official website, followed its Docker installation guide, and pulled the required image.

The official setup uses a single Docker container with persistent storage, so I didn’t need to configure PostgreSQL or Redis separately. After setting the required environment variables and port mappings, I started the container and accessed Baserow in my browser. The entire process took around 10 minutes.

From there, I created my account, set up a workspace, and started experimenting with databases. I could create tables from scratch, use ready-made templates, or import existing information from CSV and Excel files.

A simple and easy-to-use UI

You won’t have a hard time getting started

One thing I immediately appreciated about Baserow was its clean and intuitive user interface. Despite being a powerful database platform, it doesn’t bombard me with unnecessary menus, complicated settings, or technical terms.

Everything is neatly organized, and if you have ever worked with Notion databases, Airtable, or even a traditional spreadsheet, you will feel right at home.

The main interface has a familiar spreadsheet-like layout, with records arranged in rows and fields in columns. I can create new tables, add custom fields, rearrange columns, and organize information without digging through endless menus.

For instance, when I created a database to manage my editorial calendar, I simply added columns for article titles, publication dates, categories, priorities, and publishing status. I also like how Baserow keeps everything accessible from a sidebar.

Switching between databases and tables feels effortless, and I don’t have to constantly navigate through multiple pages to find what I need.

I recreated my Notion databases effortlessly

And they are way better than Obsidian

One of the first things I did after setting up Baserow was recreate my existing Notion databases, and the experience was smooth. I started with my editorial calendar, where I track article ideas, deadlines, and overall progress. Baserow gave me plenty of customization options to build a database that worked exactly how I wanted.

Another useful feature is the ability to create different views of the same database. I could stick with the familiar spreadsheet-style Grid view or switch to Gallery view for a more visual presentation. Baserow also supports conditional row coloring with its Premium plan, which adds another layer of visual organization.

While Obsidian Bases is excellent for managing structured Markdown notes, I found Baserow better suited to my database-heavy workflows, especially when dealing with linked tables and customized fields.

And unlike my Notion and Trello setups, Baserow runs directly on my own hardware through Docker. My databases don’t need to reside on someone else’s cloud server. Of course, securing and maintaining the server is my responsibility, but that’s a trade-off I am happy to make.

I'm never going back to Notion after mastering this open-source self-hosted tool

A tool that's already powerful, made even better by self-hosting it

5
By  Nolen Jonker

Automation takes productivity another level higher

Ideal for power users

This is where Baserow started to impress me. Organizing information is one thing, but automating repetitive tasks takes the experience to an entirely different level. Baserow comes with a built-in Automation builder that lets me create custom workflows without writing a single line of code.

The concept is simple. I can define a trigger, specify conditions, and choose what happens next. For instance, I can configure a workflow around my editorial calendar so that whenever an article’s status changes to Ready to Editing, Baserow automatically sends a notification to the relevant person.

I also appreciate the visual workflow builder. Instead of dealing with complicated scripts, I can connect triggers and actions, add conditional logic, and test everything before publishing the automation. It supports scheduled triggers, database changes, HTTP requests, and integrations with external services.

This is exactly what my fragmented productivity setup was missing. Rather than constantly switching between apps and manually updating information, I can let Baserow handle repetitive tasks while I focus on writing and other meaningful work.

One self-hosted tool does it all

I didn’t expect a single Docker container to replace three of my favorite productivity tools, but Baserow came quite close. Of course, it isn’t a perfect replacement for every Notion or Obsidian feature, and some advanced capabilities require a paid plan.

However, if your workflow revolves around structured information and project tracking, it’s a compelling alternative. If you are tired of juggling productivity apps, this is one Docker container that deserves a closer look.

Baserow

Baserow is an open-source alternative to Airtable and Trello.

item.title: I've tried countless gamepads over the years, but nothing has topped the Xbox 360 controller
item.itunes:title: I've tried countless gamepads over the years, but nothing has topped the Xbox 360 controller
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Since its launch, the Xbox 360 controller has been the gold standard for PC gaming (and, frankly, a bar every console controller needs to meet). If you've ever used one, it's not hard to see why; the Xbox 360 controller fits most hands comfortably — yes, even the tiny ones — and is incredibly durable.

While the controllers had their fair share of design faults, like bumpers that would get stuck or cords that would wear out, plenty stillwork after years of use. Show me an Xbox Elite controller that's still working that smoothly.

I still use an Xbox 360 controller as my primary PC gaming device. I've tried others, but it just doesn't feel the same. Maybe it's nostalgia. Maybe it's just that I've used a 360 controller for so long that anything else feels wrong. Either way, it still stands as the best PC gaming controller ever made.

It works out of the box with most computers

That's slightly less impressive now, but it was a big deal when it first launched

Here's the thing: two decades ago, fewer PC games supported controllers. The gamepads available were clunky and hard to use, often requiring software that needed a degree in theoretical physics and dark magic to make sense of. The Xbox 360 controller supported XInput auto-mapping on most Windows devices, meaning the inputs were automatically read when you plugged it in. You didn't need complicated software to map key bindings to the controller.

In 2026, that might not seem like that big of a deal. Controller support is far more widespread now, especially with PC receiving one-time console exclusives. But even now, the Xbox 360 controller is one of the easiest and most reliable gamepads on the market, and you can connect it to almost any modern Windows device, and it will work seamlessly.

Someone modded their Steam Deck to look like an Xbox 360 handheld, and I'm in love

It's amazing what a few tweaks can do.

By  Simon Batt

It's comfortable for extended use

My hands don't hurt after long play sessions

There were times I could spend all day playing a video game, but that depended heavily on the console. If you've ever tried playing an NES for hours on end, good luck with the hand cramps. Even the original PlayStation was rough in that regard; it took a few years for the PlayStation 4's ergonomics to catch up.

The Xbox 360 controller was comfortable and seemed built to fit an actual human hand, unlike the "Duke" controller of the original Xbox. It was unnecessarily large and outweighed only by the console itself. The Xbox 360 controller's sleek design was a breath of fresh air after that, and it still holds up well even as other brands have caught up in design.

It's affordable

Third-party and used controllers are easy to come by

As far as I'm concerned, the Xbox 360 controller is near the peak of gamepad design. While the advanced features of the Xbox Elite controller are awesome, I mostly use them in FPS games — and if I'm playing an FPS on PC, I'll use a mouse and keyboard. The only other time I ever used the paddles was in racing games that required manual shifting, and that was pretty rare. Since I can get a decent third-party Xbox 360 controller for my PC for around $20, compared to spending at least three times that for a modern gamepad, the winner is clear.

All those extra features are nice, but for most players they're not worth the dramatically higher cost. If you play a lot of console games, the Xbox Elite controller is an amazing investment, but I can't recommend one over a standard gamepad for PC players.

The Xbox 360 controller is starting to show its age

20 years of innovation isn't nothing

As much as I love the Xbox 360 controller (and still largely recommend it), a few issues need addressing. First is that there's no Bluetooth. If you're using an original Xbox 360 wireless controller, you need a dedicated Xbox 360 receiver to use it with PCs. Wired variants are more readily available, but the cable can be annoying. And that points to the biggest issue: outdated hardware. There's no USB-C support, and if you're using a wireless model, you'll go through a lot of batteries.

However, the biggest issue is the D-pad. Many gamers use a gamepad for emulation, and the Xbox 360 controller's D-pad was built as an enhanced interrogation tool. It's a little small for my tastes, has mushy inputs, and lacks the precision needed for platformers and fighting games. Seriously, try playing Celeste on a 360 controller if you want to test your sanity.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller seen above is, objectively, a more powerful, more functional controller, but new isn't always better.

Good design never goes out of style

The Xbox 360 controller proves that good design doesn't go out of style and that newer doesn't always mean better. Sure, there are incredibly customizable controllers out there, but for the average person? The Xbox 360 controller is hard to beat. The fact that I've used it for this many years and haven't felt the need to upgrade is a testament to that.

Sony and Microsoft need to learn the lesson Nintendo has been teaching since the 1983 crash

Cheaper hardware, better games, happier consumers.

item.title: I ran Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor on the same AI model, and the tool mattered more than I expected
item.itunes:title: I ran Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor on the same AI model, and the tool mattered more than I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I write about AI coding agents a lot, and somewhere along the way I'd decided the model was doing all the heavy lifting. Swap Claude Code for Codex or Cursor, keep the same brain underneath, and you should get the same work back. So I put that to the test.

I gave all three Claude Sonnet 5.5 at high reasoning, the same buggy WebSocket proxy that feeds my Kindle data from Home Assistant, 30 minutes, and $10 each. Every one of them scored a perfect 16 out of 16 on the final code, but that's the last thing they had in common.

I tried DeepSeek's agent harness, and it's not the Claude Code clone I expected

Everything is a plugin, and I mean everything

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Making three tools use the same model was harder than expected

At least, without upgrading some subscription plans

You'd think that choosing the model would be the easy part, but it turned out to be more complicated than I expected. We've tested these three tools extensively with the default models, but to create a more controlled experiment I wanted to reduce the variables.

There are no models that are native to Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, which meant that at least one of the tools would have to use their model through a translation layer. I also wanted to stick to documented official routes, and that kept pointing in one direction.

Cursor uses a subscription model, and you need one to use third-party models. That's anything but Grok, just in case you needed a reminder. Codex has a supported route using OpenRouter as the endpoint for third-party models. And while Claude Code can use third party models, it was built to only talk to Claude, so other models introduce a second translation layer that none of the providers guarantees will work.

That last point really was the decider, at least for testing these three tools objectively. If Claude Code only guarantees runs to work with Claude models, then that's it. Cursor has Sonnet 5.5 via API credits, and Codex supports OpenRouter, so I could use API calls there too. Cursor and Codex defaulted to high reasoning, so I had to change Claude Code's default of medium, and then all three tools used the same model with the same setup.

The job before them

I already had a project for the agents to work on. The Kindle dashboard for Home Assistant that I'd ported from the supported Kindle Paperwhite version to the device I actually own. It already has four bugs that I had been meaning to fix, plus I wanted an auto-reconnect feature for the proxy server. There's also another trap, because the Kindle is so old it only supports ECMAScript 5. That means no modern JavaScript conveniences to use, and plenty of room for the agentic coding tools to get something wrong.

I also added a second prompt with a request for new features, Home Assistant status messages and an offline badge to alert me if the server went down. This was scored using a 16 test routine that was deliberately kept out of the folders the agentic tools could use, because I've learned that a test the agent can see is one that it will write around to pass even if the code doesn't work for the intended use.

My Proxmox server now runs a full dev environment for AI agents, and it's surprisingly easy to manage

I brought the cloud, home.

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

All three passed my testing suite

The model decided what got built, including some features I didn't ask for

If you were expecting one of the tools to fail, you're going to be disappointed. All three used the same model, and the finished code passed all of my tests. It passed all the additional tests that the harness wrote along the way, although each of the tools decided on different tests to check its own work.

The change to the dashboard was almost identical between the tools, and both Codex and Claude Code used the same function name to build it with. That pattern held for the reconnect fix as well, with the same names used by the same model in three different tools. That's an underlying fingerprint of Sonnet 5.5, not a quirk of the harnesses used.

When fixing the Kindle proxy module, Codex kept most of the original code, deciding that it would patch it instead of rewriting. Both Cursor and Claude Code restructured it into smaller methods. Cursor kept 43% of the original code and said that it rewrote the file in its summary, while Claude Code stripped it back to 34% of the original.

All three tools also added the same unrequested extras. A banner that shows when the Kindle loses connection to the proxy. Fixes for a malformed JSON crash and a return-vs-continue bug, along with a check on the status of the proxy when first connected. None of these were in the TASK.md planning document in the working folder, but it's interesting to see the same model come to the same conclusions about fixing bugs across multiple tools.

Wherever the job was small and clear, the same model wrote almost identical code across the three tools. Where it differed was in open-ended questions, things like how much of an existing file to restructure, how much defensive code to add, and how much additional testing to build.

One other interesting fact. The original repo for the Kindle dashboard was in German. Codex and Cursor used German when rewriting the UI elements of the dashboard, while Claude Code wrote English. Not a huge worry either way, as you could ask the agent to change to your preferred language, and I don't want to speculate as to why each tool handled it the way they did.

Claude orchestrating Codex agents is the workflow I didn't know I needed for coding

Trust, but verify (and let the agents verify too)

6
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Where the tools actually split

Speed, self-checks, and quirks

Think about the last time you had to use a rental car, rather than the one you're used to driving daily. Same driver, different vehicle, and same daily commute. Except it's never exactly the same, is it? Your driving habits are one thing, but fuel economy, ergonomics, and other things come into play.

And that's analagous to what happened here. Sonnet 5.5 wrote almost the same code regardless of what it was driving, but the overall experience was different. Not meaningfully enough that I could say objectively which of the three tools is better, but enough that I have strong feelings over which one I prefer.

And Claude Code ended up running 42 tests because it ran the same suite three times to ensure accuracy. Claude Code also put the original bug back into the code, to ensure that the tests it wrote caught the issue. It didn't matter on this occasion, but on messier, larger codebases that could have been the decider between working output code and not.

Both Claude Code and Codex finished before the ten-minute mark for the first test, which meant only Cursor got to test how steering worked with the second prompt. Except, it didn't test steering at all because, by default, it queues the next command instead. I could have changed that, but I wanted to test defaults wherever I could.

And all three tools needed some setup time to get them to behave on Windows. Codex ignored the --ask-for-approval flag until I added it to the TOML settings file, then the server crashed because it couldn't launch PowerShell without an environment value being set. Claude Code prefers Bash, so I had to set a flag for it to use PowerShell instead of it trying to use WSL. Cursor opened the run in ask for approval mode, even though I had set it to auto.

Pricing wise, it's probably not a surprise that Claude Code was the cheapest to use Sonnet 5.5 with. What I didn't expect was that Codex would pay full price for its OpenRouter method, with seemingly no tokens coming from cache reads. And Cursor might have made me pay for the $30 premium plan to run third-party models via an additional API billing cost, but it looks like it cached tokens because I paid $1.11 for roughly 3.31 million tokens, compared to $3.73 for 1.64 million tokens on Codex/OpenRouter. The only way that math works is if most of those Cursor reads were from the cache.

I gave Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor the same complex web app to build, but only one worked like a senior developer

The difference was in the details.

item.title: I turned off constant polling in my automations, and Home Assistant finally ran cool
item.itunes:title: I turned off constant polling in my automations, and Home Assistant finally ran cool
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you set up an automation in Home Assistant, you focus most of your attention on getting it to work. And once everything works, you move on to something else. How often an automation checks a sensor or sends requests to a device rarely gets the same attention, especially when you're still experimenting with your setup.

But as your smart home grows, that background activity deserves a closer look. I've been revisiting my own setup, cutting down on unnecessary polling and being more selective about when automations run and what Home Assistant records. My system now runs cooler and responds faster.

Your automations keep checking things that haven’t changed

They absolutely don't need to do that

Time-based triggers are a convenient way to get an automation working in Home Assistant. The problem is they keep running on a schedule, even if nothing has changed. Your room could be empty for hours, but the automation would still keep checking whether anyone is there.

Now, checking a sensor's existing value doesn't require much processing power on its own. The problem starts when those checks also refresh devices, evaluate complex templates, or repeatedly send the same commands. If the lights are already off, there's absolutely no reason to keep telling them to switch off every few minutes just because the room is still empty.

Fortunately, Home Assistant supports state-based triggers, so your automations can run when something actually changes. For example, instead of checking whether a room is empty every few minutes, you can trigger an automation when the occupancy sensor detects that nobody has been there for two minutes. Similarly, if you're using a temperature-based automation to control a fan, you can have it trigger when the temperature crosses a certain threshold instead of constantly checking the reading.

This is usually where I start when reviewing my automations. I look at what each automation is checking and whether I can use a state change to trigger it directly. Of course, scheduled checks still have their place, especially for periodic updates or catching missed issues.

5 useful Home Assistant automations I wish I had in my life sooner

From energy tracking to turning off devices when not in use, Home Assistant helps improve my life by automating my smart home.

5
By  Samir Makwana

Offline devices don’t need constant attention

You don't need to waste your resources on these devices

Some smart home devices can spend hours switched off or disconnected. The problem starts when your automations keep trying to communicate with these devices even though they're offline. Sending the same command every few seconds accomplishes nothing, and repeated failures can clutter your logs.

Home Assistant lets you check whether an entity is available before running an action. If a device is unavailable or its state is unknown, the automation can skip commands meant for that device. This is particularly useful for routines involving multiple devices. If one device is offline, the entire routine doesn't need to fail or keep trying to reach it. The other devices can still do their jobs.

But there's another thing worth looking at here — how often Home Assistant polls these devices in the first place. Adding an availability check to an automation doesn't change how frequently an integration contacts a device. For integrations that support it, you can disable automatic polling and use homeassistant.update_entity to request updates at intervals that make sense. For example, if you only need a sensor's reading every 15 minutes, there's little reason to refresh it every few seconds.

You do need to be careful about recovery, though. Some integrations rely on polling to discover when a device comes back online. If you stop polling entirely, Home Assistant might never realize the device is available again. I prefer keeping a slower periodic check or using another trigger, such as a smart plug switching back on, to request an update. Once the device is available, the automation can check whether it still needs to do anything.

You don’t need to act on every update

Some can be safely ignored

Another thing I've learned from using Home Assistant is that you don't always want an automation to respond the moment something changes. Sensors aren't perfect, and their readings can fluctuate quite a bit. For example, a presence sensor might briefly report that a room is empty even when you're sitting right there. If your automation reacts immediately, the lights could switch off for no reason. The same happens with appliances that report power consumption, where readings can jump up and down throughout their operation.

A simple way to handle this is to make sure a condition stays true for a set amount of time before triggering an action. Take a washing machine, for example. You can set up an automation to notify you when its power consumption drops below a certain threshold. But washing machines can briefly stop drawing significant power between stages, so you don't want a notification every time that happens. Instead, you can require the power consumption to stay below that threshold for three or five minutes before Home Assistant considers the cycle finished.

Similarly, I prefer giving my presence sensors a couple of minutes to confirm that a room is empty before switching off the lights. You're deliberately adding a small delay, but it makes these automations much more reliable. I've also started paying more attention to what Home Assistant stores in its database. Many sensors update frequently, and although I want to see their current readings on my dashboard, I don't necessarily need Home Assistant to keep a history of every change.

There's also a setting called commit_interval in Recorder that lets you control how frequently Home Assistant commits changes to its database. Increasing this interval can reduce disk I/O by grouping more writes, but the trade-off is that Home Assistant could lose more recent updates if it crashes before committing.

Your older automations deserve another look

Home Assistant is already pretty efficient, but unnecessary background activity adds up as your smart home grows. I've found that revisiting older automations, reducing polling, and cleaning up database recording can make a noticeable difference. If you've been running Home Assistant for a while, it's worth checking what your automations are doing.

I replaced my smart bulbs with smart relays and saved my family from home automation fatigue

Your smart home shouldn't cause friction.

Some smart home devices can spend hours switched off or disconnected. The problem starts when your automations keep trying to communicate with these devices even though they're offline. Sending the same command every few seconds accomplishes nothing, and repeated failures can clutter your logs.

Home Assistant lets you check whether an entity is available before running an action. If a device is unavailable or its state is unknown, the automation can skip commands meant for that device. This is particularly useful for routines involving multiple devices. If one device is offline, the entire routine doesn't need to fail or keep trying to reach it. The other devices can still do their jobs.

But there's another thing worth looking at here — how often Home Assistant polls these devices in the first place. Adding an availability check to an automation doesn't change how frequently an integration contacts a device. For integrations that support it, you can disable automatic polling and use homeassistant.update_entity to request updates at intervals that make sense. For example, if you only need a sensor's reading every 15 minutes, there's little reason to refresh it every few seconds.

You do need to be careful about recovery, though. Some integrations rely on polling to discover when a device comes back online. If you stop polling entirely, Home Assistant might never realize the device is available again. I prefer keeping a slower periodic check or using another trigger, such as a smart plug switching back on, to request an update. Once the device is available, the automation can check whether it still needs to do anything.

Some can be safely ignored

Another thing I've learned from using Home Assistant is that you don't always want an automation to respond the moment something changes. Sensors aren't perfect, and their readings can fluctuate quite a bit. For example, a presence sensor might briefly report that a room is empty even when you're sitting right there. If your automation reacts immediately, the lights could switch off for no reason. The same happens with appliances that report power consumption, where readings can jump up and down throughout their operation.

A simple way to handle this is to make sure a condition stays true for a set amount of time before triggering an action. Take a washing machine, for example. You can set up an automation to notify you when its power consumption drops below a certain threshold. But washing machines can briefly stop drawing significant power between stages, so you don't want a notification every time that happens. Instead, you can require the power consumption to stay below that threshold for three or five minutes before Home Assistant considers the cycle finished.

You're deliberately adding a small delay, but it makes these automations much more reliable. I've also started paying more attention to what Home Assistant stores in its database. Many sensors update frequently, and although I want to see their current readings on my dashboard, I don't necessarily need Home Assistant to keep a history of every change.

There's also a setting called commit_interval in Recorder that lets you control how frequently Home Assistant commits changes to its database. Increasing this interval can reduce disk I/O by grouping more writes, but the trade-off is that Home Assistant could lose more recent updates if it crashes before committing.

Your older automations deserve another look

Home Assistant is already pretty efficient, but unnecessary background activity adds up as your smart home grows. I've found that revisiting older automations, reducing polling, and cleaning up database recording can make a noticeable difference. If you've been running Home Assistant for a while, it's worth checking what your automations are doing.

item.itunes:title: I changed one llama.cpp flag, and my 8GB laptop GPU now runs a 35B model faster than I can read
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A lot of what you can do with your PC seems to be limited by the VRAM its GPU has. It decides what resolution your games run at, how large a video project you can edit without the timeline stuttering intermittently, and most recently, which local AI models you can self-host. A lot of these examples feel like hard limits, but there are workarounds for almost all of them.

Perhaps the simplest of those workarounds relate to local AI inference. I had already mentally disqualified my Lenovo Legion 5 with an 8GB RTX 3070 Mobile GPU from running some of the models that I run on my RTX 4070 Ti Super with 16GB of GDDR6X. However, in the past couple weeks of testing, I stumbled upon a workaround that helps it to run massive models itself at reasonable speeds.

One llama.cpp flag had my curiosity

Were the best models truly reserved for bigger GPUs, or was there a workaround?

Last week, I talked about moving my local AI stack from Ollama to llama.cpp, and while testing the runtime and its various features, it struck me that one of those features can help optimize a smaller system with a lower VRAM budget to run models that have absolutely no business running on it. On my desktop's RTX 4070 Ti Super, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B was the fastest model I tested at IQ4_XS quantization and 32K context, despite being a whopping 17.7GB file sitting on top of 16GB of GDDR6X.

The math says the model shouldn't fit the VRAM, of course, but Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models already changed the math a while back. Out of the model's 35 billion parameters, roughly only 3 billion are activated for inference and the rest sit idle. Much of the trick is moving the dormant expert layers to the system RAM while the always-on parts of the network stay comfortably resident on the GPU.

The flag that makes this possible is --n-cpu-moe N. You can pair it with -ngl 99 to instruct llama.cpp to load every layer to the GPU, and --n-cpu-moe then peels expert tensors of the first N layers back off and keeps them in system RAM. As a result, attention layers, embeddings, shared weights and most importantly the KV cache all stay in VRAM, which are all integral to token generation speeds. The expert layers, on the other hand, are only touched when the router picks them, are resident in the system memory, and get copied over as needed.

This naturally got me curious about my Lenovo laptop. If a 17.7GB model can run on a system with 16GB of VRAM, exactly how far can the same trick stretch a system with 8GB of VRAM? That was precisely the question driving the experiment I've detailed.

I ditched cloud AI for these 3 local models, and my 8GB GPU handles them all

8GB may not be great for games, but it can be more than enough for these local models

1
By  Abhinav Raj

Llama-bench had all the information I needed to fine-tune the model

It took one command to see if my laptop's 8GB GPU could hold up

Prior to using any flags, I wanted an honest and reproducible answer to check if my 8GB RTX 3070 laptop GPU could actually sustain inference on something larger than the models it was built for. I would argue that there's no better way to check it than llama.cpp's utility known as llama-bench.

For this test, I ran both the models I have on my laptop, including Qwen3.6-27B at IQ4_XS quantization and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at UD-IQ4_XS quantization. If you're wondering why I used a dense model that can't have expert layers offloaded to the RAM, it's because it is used as a reference to benchmark against. To start the test, I used the following command:

.\llama-bench.exe -m Qwen3.6-27B-IQ4_XS.gguf -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf -ngl 99 -ncmoe 0,28 -p 512 -n 128 -r 3 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0

This benchmarks four configurations on both models, each at --n-cpu-moe 0 (no offload), and 28 (28 layers' worth of expert weights moved to system RAM). It's worth taking a moment to understand what each flag means here.

The -ngl 99 instructs llama.cpp to attempt loading every layer onto the GPU. The -p 512 -n 128 sets a 512-token prefill followed by 128 tokens of generation per run, which are llama-bench's defaults, which are enough to produce stable numbers. Next, the -r 3 repeats each configuration three times so that singular lucky runs don't muddy up the dataset. Lastly, -ctk q8_0 - ctv q8_0 quantizes the KV cache down to 8-bit.

The following are the results llama-bench produced after the run.

Not applicable (Dense model)

32.82

One llama.cpp flag turned my 8GB laptop into a 35B inference machine

A desktop optimization unlocked an entirely different tier on my laptop

For the longest time, just like most other users, my mental model of local AI was simple, yet deceptive. I thought that only my desktop could run the serious models, and the laptop would have to stick with whatever small Gemma 4 variants could fit in the VRAM. This experiment has completely subverted that expectation in perhaps the best way possible.

It is, indeed, possible to optimize a 35B mixture-of-experts model that barely crosses 4 tokens/second to do 33 tokens per second on the very same hardware with the use of flags. Roughly 33 tokens per second is much faster than I read, which means the model responds at a speed that I am comfortable working with.

Two old GPUs I salvaged are doing more AI work than a brand new $2000 card, and I won't be upgrading anytime soon

I built a local AI setup out of two old GPUs that sell for cheap, and it beats a single new card

3
By  Ayush Pande

The best models aren't reserved for my desktop anymore

Perhaps the one thing that this optimization changes in a way that it matters to me, and I'd wager would matter to most users like myself, is the level of access it enables. Most users would think loading up a 35B MoE model would mean sitting at home at their desks right next to their workstations, but with the right flags and right optimizations, it's possible to carry a 35B model on the go, no matter whether it's on a flight, in a hotel, or a place with no network. That is something significant that llama.cpp enables for me.

item.title: I ditched 4 expensive desktop apps for free open-source alternatives, and I wish I'd done it sooner
item.itunes:title: I ditched 4 expensive desktop apps for free open-source alternatives, and I wish I'd done it sooner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Paying for third-party apps is something we've all become used to, one way or another. Whether it's to fulfill work commitments or satisfy creative interests, app subscriptions now constitute a significant portion of our monthly expenses. Video editing, photo editing, note-taking, cloud storage, document editing, and antivirus are some of the areas where people prefer the convenience and features of paid software.

After paying a considerable sum in subscriptions over the last few years, I decided to give open-source alternatives a serious try, and I was surprised how smooth the transition was. From password management and document management to video and photo editing, I'm now using free apps that do all I need for work, hobbies, or security. The benefit to my wallet is a sweet bonus, too.

4 lightweight open-source tools that replaced all of my paid apps

Free, fast, and fully capable

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Bitwarden: I don't need paid password managers

Moving away from Google doesn't need to be expensive

Like many others, my online activity was deeply entangled with Google's Password Manager before I thought about migrating to something more secure and private. Google's solution is seamless and convenient, especially for an Android and Chrome user like myself, but it had started to feel limiting. I was ready to transition to a better solution, even if it meant paying for it.

I moved to 1Password for a while, as it was the one most of my friends were using at the time. It cost me about $30–$40 a year, but its auto password generation, autofill capability, and cross-platform support felt worth it. Besides, 1Password had a strong audit history and used a zero-knowledge architecture, which meant only I had access to my password vault.

Then, I discovered Bitwarden and never looked back. Even without the paid tier, I could enjoy all the 1Password features I just listed above. It had everything I needed to safely store, use, and share my passwords. I was saving money without compromising on security, which is always a win. You can self-host Vaultwarden instead, a community-driven version of Bitwarden that's lighter and brings free TOTP, which is paid on Bitwarden.

Bitwarden
OS
Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, others (browser extension)

Bitwarden is a free, open-source password manager that's available across different platforms, and works well without any issues. The free version of Bitwarden comes with all the essentials, but you can also upgrade to the paid version for some added features.

See at Microsoft Store See at Chrome Web Store See at Bitwarden

Adopt these apps for a simple, more private digital life

2
By  Parth Shah

LibreOffice: I'm never paying for Microsoft 365 again

It beats Microsoft where it hurts

For most of us, Microsoft Office has been part of our lives since childhood, and it's hard to escape its clutches. Most of the world still uses it, businesses depend on it, and most of us are too familiar with it to switch to something else. I found myself in the same boat, but when Microsoft increased prices early last year, I was determined to find a free alternative that did most of what I depended on Microsoft for.

LibreOffice was the answer, since it was an open-source suite that satisfied my document, spreadsheet, and presentation needs. I was finally free of Microsoft's forced AI bloat and expensive subscription fee. I realized I wasn't using much of the Microsoft 365 offering anyway, so moving to LibreOffice was actually the sensible choice.

The open-source office alternative uses the OpenDocument format (ODF) and supports Microsoft Office formats as well. It's cross-platform and features customizable toolbars that offer a seamless transition from Office. Most of my work happens online on Google Docs now, so LibreOffice is more than enough for my occasional offline document editing.

Free
Platforms
Windows, macOS, Linux

LibreOffice is one of the most complete Microsoft Office alternatives, and it's entirely free and open-source. It gives you various different tools for various use cases, including Math and Draw tools for advanced users.

I thought free office suites always came with compromises, but this open-source tool proved I was completely wrong.

1
By  Yash Patel

Kdenlive: It's more powerful than what I need

Goodbye, Premiere Pro

Video editing is one job many of us keep coming back to — it's just so embedded in our digital lives today. I'm not a content creator, but I still need to edit the occasional product or marketing video for my business or refine an Instagram reel every few weeks. While Adobe Premiere Pro was my default choice for years, it was starting to get too pricey for my needs. That realization brought me to Kdenlive.

It was one of the most popular tools used by fellow XDA writers, and after using it for a few days, I quickly learned why. It supports all the basics like multi-track editing, non-destructive editing, color correction, and hardware acceleration. With proxy editing to work with heavy files and wide format support, I don't need any other tool for my video editing needs.

While the individual Premiere Pro subscription isn't prohibitively expensive (yet), I don't want to pay unless it's absolutely needed. After realizing that Kdenlive can do most of what Premiere Pro does for free, I don't think I'd want to go back. As for the other Creative Cloud apps, I have another thing coming in the next section.

If you love Premiere Pro but hate the subscription, try Kdenlive

2
By  Nolen Jonker

PhotoCraft: Vibe-coded Photoshop is actually good

AI isn't all bad, right?

Photoshop was the other big reason I had been subscribed to Adobe's Creative Cloud for a long time. Our projects were created in Photoshop, and the team was used to working in Adobe's ecosystem. However, when news started circulating about AI-created clones of Adobe's most popular apps, I couldn't resist checking the project out. Developer Brandon Thomas had used years of experience and Claude Opus to recreate Adobe's CC suite.

PhotoCraft is the vibe-coded Photoshop alternative that we've been using for a few weeks. It looks almost identical to Adobe's solution and offers much of the functionality, too. Since the layout is the same and it allows working on PSD files, we're surprised how smooth the transition has been. Although advanced tools like Generative Fill and Generative Expand aren't there yet, PhotoCraft is still impressive given that it's free and a work in progress.

FOSS doesn't mean inferior

The assumption that free and open-source alternatives are always inferior to paid alternatives hasn't been true for a while. People have started to value privacy more than ever, and ditching expensive subscriptions is more possible than ever. When free video editing, photo editing, and document processing apps offer 90% of the functionality for free, people are bound to take notice.

item.title: 5 ESP32 projects that make dumb appliances smart without opening them up
item.itunes:title: 5 ESP32 projects that make dumb appliances smart without opening them up
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Building a smart home is great until you come across a dumb appliance. My first instinct is to grab a screwdriver, open it up, understand the internals, and plug an ESP32 into it. But that also means voiding the warranty and soldering it. It’s natural to dread the soldering part because no one wants to risk it on an expensive appliance.

Over time, I’ve found a better way to use an ESP32 with a dumb or non-smart appliance with Home Assistant. After all, plenty of ESP32 projects give old gadgets a second life. You can take a slightly different approach for each ESP32 board to make the appliance smart without opening anything.

6 projects you can complete in a weekend with the $5 ESP32

The ESP32 is affordable and powerful, and there's a lot you can do with one.

3
By  Adam Conway

A door and lid monitor

A simple sensor can tell you when the door is left open

I realized I am not the only one who sometimes leaves the wardrobe, a cabinet, or even the chest freezer open. Double-checking is good, but it’s also helpful to have a prompt that tells you if you or someone else has left it open. All you need is a cheap magnetic reed switch with a mini ESP32 board like a C3 or S3. The switch has two pieces, a magnet and a sensor, mounted separately.

Mount one half on the door and the other on the frame, power the board with a single coin-cell battery, and program it to sleep deeply when it’s not needed. You don’t need the door reporting a closed state all day. The board only needs to wake up if it detects the door open for a minute or more.

ESP32-S3

ESP32-S3 comes with a dual-core Xtensa LX7 microcontroller. It has 16MB of flash memory and 8MB of PSRAM with years of maturity to be ready for a variety of projects.

See at Amazon

A Bluetooth proxy range extender

Locate devices and trigger automations using BLE

Building a Bluetooth proxy revealed all the chatty Bluetooth Low Energy devices in my home. But some still weren’t part of the network, like my electric toothbrush, lights, or window blinds. Whether I’m using a Philips Sonicare or an Oral-B Smart Series, it has Bluetooth to talk to a mobile app. Running a Bluetooth Proxy on an ESP32 lets the toothbrush act as a beacon to trigger bathroom-specific automations. Of course, the house gets smarter, not the toothbrush. It sounds ridiculous, but it’s a genuine “why not” project, thanks to the open-source Bermuda project, instead of just a “what if” idea.

A vibration sensor flags a finished wash cycle

Without touching the machine, know when the laundry’s ready

You don’t need a timer for repetitive tasks like knowing when a washing machine cycle ends. An ESP32 board with a vibration sensor can tell you exactly when that happens. You’re free from manually checking the wash cycle, and you’ll know the instant the laundry’s ready to come out. You can use ESPHome to write the firmware for ESP32 that watches for that movement and figure out when the machine has finished running. Of course, you might need to tweak the configuration so that you don’t get notified in between the wash and rinse cycles.

DIY smart speakers and a network streamer

You’ll need a specific ESP32 board or a few components to piece it all together

You don’t need to replace your old speakers with new smart ones just to control them from your phone. Plus, that’s a costly upgrade, and you can get similar functionality without emptying your wallet. The easiest route is the ESP32-A1S audio kit. It comes with line-in support, and flashing it with Squeezelite-ESP32 turns it into a DIY Bluetooth or network speaker. Set the ESP32 board as your streaming target, and apps like Spotify or your media server can send audio directly to your old speakers. Honestly, that’s a project worth undertaking before splurging on multi-room smart speakers.

An IR blaster replaces every remote in the house

Control the AC, TV, fan, and other systems that still use infrared

Home Assistant recently added infrared support, which has helped me bring my old TV, AC, and remote-controlled fan into Home Assistant. I’m currently building and testing a universal IR remote transmitter for my home. For that, I’m wiring up a couple of IR LEDs to an ESP32 through a small transistor on a basic hobby circuit board. I’m still working on placement so the transmitter points at the AC, TV, fan, and other electronics without obstruction. But that’s only half of it, because I need the ESP32 to learn to replay the received signal when I press a specific key on the remote, record that information, and relay it to the target device on command.

By storing that information, I can flash ESPHome firmware that easily triggers Home Assistant automations, like turning on the AC before I get home. You can use the same logic across several ESP32 projects to replace commercial products many people pay for, except the most common one is a universal remote you’d have to program anyway.

7 sensors under $10 that completely changed my smart home

You don't need to splurge to build a smart home

29
By  Samir Makwana

You don’t need a screwdriver and soldering kit

These five projects use an ESP32 to treat the appliance as a sealed unit, not something you need to open. A couple of these projects require some extra work to get the configuration right. But it’s still easier than reverse-engineering an appliance’s internals. None of them risk turning an appliance into a very expensive paperweight. If you’ve been meaning to make your home smarter, you can pair up an ESP32 with an old appliance without opening it up.

item.title: I switched from Google TV to Apple TV 4K, and the privacy improvements alone were worth it
item.itunes:title: I switched from Google TV to Apple TV 4K, and the privacy improvements alone were worth it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My TV is one of the most-used screens in my home. I like playing vintage horror movies in the background while I work. But what I don’t like is that modern televisions across the board serve as advertising platforms (I’m looking at you, Google TV) or even spyware, as we recently found out with LG. I'm not a fan of that at all.

Look, Google TV is convenient with great recommendations, content discovery, and AI integrations, but it is hard to ignore just how deep the Google services and advertising rabbit hole goes. Since it’s basically impossible to switch it all off, I switched to an Apple TV 4K. I wanted a cleaner interface, but I also got much more control over how my data is used and what happens to my viewing habits. There's no going back.

Apple makes it easy to manage app tracking and data sharing

Google TV collects way more data than I'm comfortable sharing

There's no denying that Google TV is an excellent platform. And its core functionality is pretty great. For people who don't want to invest in a streamer, or just want to stick within Google's ecosystem with a Google TV box, it offers an effective way to get recommendations from all their streaming services and beyond. The problem is that this convenience comes with a strong dose of data collection.

Google's TV platform can and does collect information about watch activity, installed apps, app interactions, and even approximate location to personalize these recommendations. You can be sure that some of this information is used for advertising as well. Look, I understand why. To give you those granular recommendations and targeted ads, it needs to know more about you. But I'm tired of every device and service building a profile on me.

The Apple TV 4K takes a refreshingly different approach to privacy controls. Head to Settings, open General, then go to Privacy & Security. From there, tap Tracking to get granular control over which apps can access details about you. By default, you have to individually grant apps permission to track you.

This matters because it ensures apps must ask permission before tracking your activity across apps from other companies for advertising or sharing information with data brokers.

You can deny individual requests or disable tracking altogether. This page also lets you disable analytics sharing with Apple and app developers. Put together, this is a massive step forward in giving you nearly full control over what information you want to share.
